key_terms.meaning: Driver and source, fiber with splices and connectors, photodiode, preamplifier and filter, decision circuit; one transmitter talks to one receiver.
Fraction of received bits decided wrongly; 10⁻⁹ is a common target, 10⁻¹² on fast links.
CNR = ½(mℛP)² ÷ [RIN(ℛP)²B + 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>D</sub>)B + 4k<sub>B</sub>TBF<sub>t</sub>/R<sub>eq</sub>]; about 50 dB for a video channel.
Peak deviation of optical power from its mean, divided by the mean.
P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M.
(P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub>) − (αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M); zero or more closes the budget.
Reserve for ageing, temperature and repairs, usually 6 dB (3 to 4 dB indoors).
Smallest and largest mean received power for the required BER; the received power must lie between them.
t<sub>chrom</sub> = |D|Lσ<sub>λ</sub>; t<sub>mod</sub> = 440L<sup>q</sup>/B<sub>0</sub> ns; t<sub>rx</sub> = 350/B<sub>rx</sub> ns (B<sub>rx</sub> in MHz).
L<sub>att</sub> = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> − joints − M)/α; L<sub>disp</sub> ≈ 0.7/(B|D|σ<sub>λ</sub>); the reach is the smaller.
α = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>) ÷ (L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub>) with the launch untouched.
z = ct/(2n), with t the round-trip time and n the group index.
NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub> = A/√(A² + 4D²), read at 5 % of peak intensity.
Wavelength above which only LP<sub>01</sub> is guided; bend-reference criterion 0.1 dB; cable cutoff ≤ 1260 nm for standard fiber.

takeaways: A point-to-point link is one chain of blocks; a digital link is judged by BER, an analog link by CNR (and CSO and CTB when it carries many channels).
Analog CNR has three noises: RIN grows with P², shot noise with P, thermal noise not at all, so a thermal-limited link loses 20 dB of CNR for every 10 dB of power lost.
The power budget subtracts every loss and a margin from P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub>; what is left is the spare, and the received power must also stay below overload.
Rise times add in quadrature, and the total must stay within 0.7 of the bit period for NRZ or 0.35 for RZ; the same rule gives the highest bit rate.
Loss sets L<sub>att</sub>, dispersion sets L<sub>disp</sub>, and the link reaches only the smaller; dispersion wins at high bit rates and with wide sources.
Cut-back attenuation keeps the launch fixed so it cancels; the OTDR measures from one end, with distance z = ct/(2n).
Dispersion is measured by pulse broadening or baseband response (bandwidth), and by pulse delay or phase shift against wavelength (chromatic D).
NA comes from the far-field cone at the 5 % level, cutoff from the bend-reference ratio at 0.1 dB, and diameter from an end-face image.
Field tests use a source and power meter for total loss, an OTDR for events (averaged from both ends), return-loss readings and a visual fault locator.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for a full power budget table and a rise-time check for one numerical link; the measurement questions want the set-up drawn, the formula, a worked reading and the precautions.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a digital point-to-point optical link and explain each block. List the system considerations that decide the choice of wavelength, fiber, source and detector.
outline: Blocks: driver and source, fiber with splices and connectors, photodiode, preamplifier and filter, decision circuit
Design starts from bit rate, distance and BER
Choices: wavelength window, multimode or single-mode fiber, LED or laser, pin or APD, with what decides each
Typical pairings by distance and rate
Both budgets must then be checked
answer: Start from the requirement. A digital point-to-point link is specified by three numbers: the bit rate B, the distance L and the bit error rate (BER) it must meet, for example 10⁻⁹. Everything else is a design choice made to meet those three.

answer.pre:
data in → [driver] → [LED or laser] → fiber + splices + connectors → [photodiode] → [preamp + filter] → [decision circuit] → data out
             P<sub>T</sub> (dBm)            loss αL + joints           I<sub>p</sub> = ℛP            bandwidth B<sub>rx</sub>         samples, decides 1/0

answer: Driver and source: the driver turns each bit into a current pulse; the LED or laser turns current into light. Its mean launched power P<sub>T</sub> (dBm), rise time t<sub>tx</sub> and spectral width σ<sub>λ</sub> enter the two budgets.
Fiber, splices and connectors: the fiber loses αL dB and spreads the pulses by dispersion; every splice (about 0.05 to 0.1 dB) and connector (0.3 to 1 dB) adds a fixed loss.
Photodiode: converts received power P to current I<sub>p</sub> = ℛP, ℛ in A/W. A pin diode is simple; an APD multiplies the current internally.

Preamplifier and filter: raise the small current and limit the bandwidth so that noise is limited; their bandwidth sets the receiver rise time t<sub>rx</sub> = 350/B<sub>rx</sub> ns (B<sub>rx</sub> in MHz).
Decision circuit: samples the filtered signal once per bit, compares it with a threshold and outputs 1 or 0. Noise at that instant causes errors, which the BER counts.

head: Choice
Options
What decides it
rows: Fiber loss (about 3, 0.4 and 0.2 dB/km) and dispersion at that window; cost of source and detector
Multimode is cheap to couple but has modal dispersion; single-mode for long or fast links
Coupled power (LED about −15 dBm, laser about 0 dBm), spectral width (40 nm, 2 nm, 0.1 nm), rise time
Sensitivity needed; an APD gains about 5 to 10 dB but needs a high bias and costs more

answer: Typical pairings: an 850 nm LED, multimode fiber and a silicon pin detector for a few kilometres at tens of Mbit/s; a 1310 nm laser on single-mode fiber for tens of kilometres; a 1550 nm DFB laser with an APD or optical amplifier for long spans at Gbit/s rates.

After choosing the parts, check two budgets. The power budget, P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> ≥ αL + joints + margin, decides whether enough light arrives. The rise-time budget, t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7/B for NRZ, decides whether the pulses stay sharp. The link passes only if both do.

Closing check with numbers: a 1 Gbit/s link at BER 10⁻⁹ makes one error per 10⁹ bits, that is one error per second on average; a 2.5 Gbit/s link at the same BER makes 2.5 errors per second, which is why faster links ask for 10⁻¹² or use error correction.

bank.q: Explain the carrier-to-noise ratio of an analog optical link and the three noise sources that limit it. A link has RIN = −143 dB/Hz, ℛ = 0.6 A/W, R<sub>eq</sub> = 750 Ω, F<sub>t</sub> = 3 dB, T = 300 K, B = 6 MHz and m = 0.5. Find the CNR for a received power of −13 dBm and say which noise dominates.
outline: Analog link: intensity follows the signal; modulation index m
Signal power ½(mℛP)²
Noise: RIN (∝ P²), shot (∝ P), thermal (independent of P)
CNR expression and its three regions
Numbers: I<sub>p</sub> = 30.1 µA; noises 0.27, 0.58, 2.65 × 10⁻¹⁶ A²; CNR 55.1 dB, thermal dominant
answer: In an analog link the laser is biased at a mean power P and the signal swings the power about that mean. The modulation index m is the peak deviation divided by the mean, so the photocurrent is I<sub>p</sub>(1 + m cos ωt) with I<sub>p</sub> = ℛP.
Signal (carrier) power: the peak signal current is mI<sub>p</sub>, so its mean-square value is ½(mI<sub>p</sub>)² = ½(mℛP)² in A².
Noise 1, relative intensity noise of the laser: ⟨i²⟩ = RIN·(ℛP)²·B. It grows as P², like the signal, so it sets a ceiling on CNR.
Noise 2, shot noise of the photodiode: ⟨i²⟩ = 2q(I<sub>p</sub> + I<sub>D</sub>)B. It grows as P.
Noise 3, thermal noise of the preamplifier load: ⟨i²⟩ = 4k<sub>B</sub>TBF<sub>t</sub>/R<sub>eq</sub>. It does not depend on P.

Three regions follow. At low power thermal noise dominates and CNR ∝ P² (20 dB per 10 dB of power). In the middle shot noise dominates and CNR ∝ P (10 dB per 10 dB). At high power RIN dominates and CNR stops rising at ½m²/(RIN·B).

Thermal noise is 2.65 of the 3.50 units, about 76 % of the total, so this receiver is thermal-noise limited: 3 dB more received power would add almost 6 dB of CNR, while a lower-RIN laser would hardly help.

Closing check: the RIN ceiling for m = 0.5 is ½m²/(RIN·B) = 0.125 ÷ (5.01 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 6 × 10⁶) = 4.16 × 10⁶, that is 66.2 dB, well above 55.1 dB, consistent with RIN being the smallest term here. A video channel needing 50 dB is met with 5.1 dB to spare.

bank.q: Define the link power budget. List every term that goes into it with typical values, and say how the result is read.
outline: P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M
P<sub>T</sub>, P<sub>R</sub> in dBm; losses and margin in dB
Fiber 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.35 to 0.5 at 1310 nm, 2.5 to 3.5 at 850 nm multimode; connector 0.3 to 1 dB; fusion splice 0.05 to 0.1 dB; margin about 6 dB
Spare = available − used; received power between sensitivity and overload
Dispersion power penalty where needed
answer: Definition: the link power budget is the account of optical power from the transmitter to the receiver. The power the transmitter launches minus the power the receiver needs must cover every loss on the route plus a reserve.

answer.pre: P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M  (+ dispersion penalty when near the dispersion limit)

head: Term
Meaning
Unit
Typical value
rows: mean power launched into the fiber
LED about −15 dBm, laser about 0 dBm
receiver sensitivity at the required BER and bit rate
pin about −30 dBm, APD about −40 dBm at hundreds of Mbit/s
system margin for ageing, temperature, repairs

answer: Unit rule: P<sub>T</sub> and P<sub>R</sub> are absolute powers in dBm; their difference and every loss are ratios in dB. A dBm value is never added to another dBm value.

Reading the result: spare = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub>) − (αL + l<sub>c</sub>N<sub>c</sub> + l<sub>s</sub>N<sub>s</sub> + M). Zero or more means the budget closes. A negative spare means a real term must change: shorter span, fewer joints, a stronger source or a more sensitive receiver; the margin is not cut to make it fit.
The received power, P<sub>T</sub> minus the physical losses only, must also stay below the receiver's overload level; a short link with a laser may need an attenuator.

Example with numbers: P<sub>T</sub> = 0 dBm, P<sub>R</sub> = −28 dBm, 60 km at 0.22 dB/km (13.2 dB), two connectors of 0.5 dB (1.0 dB), five splices of 0.1 dB (0.5 dB) and M = 6 dB. Used = 13.2 + 1.0 + 0.5 + 6 = 20.7 dB of the 28 dB available.
Closing check: spare = 28 − 20.7 = 7.3 dB, and the received power is 0 − 14.7 = −14.7 dBm, which is 13.3 dB above sensitivity: 6 dB of margin plus 7.3 dB of spare.

bank.q: A 1310 nm link has a launched power of −10 dBm, fiber loss 0.35 dB/km, length 40 km, two connectors of 0.8 dB each, four fusion splices of 0.1 dB each, receiver sensitivity −30 dBm and a system margin of 6 dB. Prepare the power budget table, decide whether the link closes, and find the longest span that passes with the same joints.
outline: Available = −10 − (−30) = 20 dB
Fiber 14 dB, connectors 1.6 dB, splices 0.4 dB, margin 6 dB: 22 dB
Spare −2 dB: the budget does not close; received power −26 dBm
Remedies without cutting the margin
answer: Available power: P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> = −10 − (−30) = 20 dB.

Decision: the spare is −2 dB, so the budget does not close. The received power would be −10 − 16 = −26 dBm. That is 4 dB above sensitivity today, so the link would work on day one, but it lacks 2 dB of the 6 dB reserve and would fail as it ages.

answer.text: Power level along the route (connector at each end, four splices spread along the 40 km):
answer.pre:
0 km, after connector 1:   −10 − 0.8 = −10.8 dBm
40 km of fiber + 4 splices:  −10.8 − 14.0 − 0.4 = −25.2 dBm
after connector 2:          −25.2 − 0.8 = −26.0 dBm
sensitivity:                −30.0 dBm  →  headroom 4.0 dB, but 6.0 dB is required

answer: Each line of the table is a loss in dB and is added; only the first two lines are absolute powers in dBm. The margin is part of the used total but not of the physical loss, which is why the received power (−26 dBm) and the spare (−2 dB) are different numbers.
Longest span. Keep the margin and the joints, and give the fiber whatever is left: 20 − 6 − 1.6 − 0.4 = 12.0 dB.
L<sub>max</sub> = 12.0 dB ÷ 0.35 dB/km = 34.3 km.

Remedies that keep the full span, with the dB each gains: a source 3 dB stronger (−7 dBm) gives +3 dB, enough; an APD receiver of about −38 dBm gives about +8 dB; moving to 1550 nm fiber at 0.22 dB/km saves 40 × (0.35 − 0.22) = 5.2 dB; better connectors (0.3 dB) save 1.0 dB, not enough alone. Cutting the margin to 4 dB would only hide the shortfall.

Rise time is not the issue here: at 1310 nm a single-mode fiber is near its zero-dispersion wavelength, so for a modest bit rate the loss, not dispersion, sets the reach. This should still be confirmed with the rise-time budget once the bit rate and source are fixed.
Closing check: at 34.3 km the received power is −10 − 12.0 − 2.0 = −24.0 dBm, which is 6.0 dB above the −30 dBm sensitivity, exactly the required margin with zero spare.

bank.q: A multimode link has rise times of 0.6 ns (source), 0.8 ns (modal), 1.2 ns (chromatic) and 0.5 ns (receiver). Find the system rise time and test it at 500 Mbit/s NRZ. What are the highest NRZ and RZ bit rates the link can carry, and which term would you attack first?
outline: 500 Mbit/s NRZ: T<sub>b</sub> = 2 ns, allowance 1.4 ns: fails
B<sub>max</sub> NRZ = 0.7/1.64 ns = 427 Mbit/s; RZ = 213 Mbit/s
Largest term chromatic: narrower source
Without the chromatic term t<sub>sys</sub> = 1.12 ns, B<sub>max</sub> = 626 Mbit/s
answer: Rule: independent rise times add in quadrature, t<sub>sys</sub> = √(t<sub>tx</sub>² + t<sub>mod</sub>² + t<sub>chrom</sub>² + t<sub>rx</sub>²). For NRZ the system rise time must not exceed 0.7T<sub>b</sub>, for RZ 0.35T<sub>b</sub>.
t<sub>sys</sub> = √2.69 = 1.640 ns.
Test at 500 Mbit/s NRZ: T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ÷ (500 × 10⁶) = 2.0 ns; allowance 0.7 × 2.0 = 1.40 ns. Since 1.640 ns > 1.40 ns, the link fails at 500 Mbit/s.
Highest NRZ rate: from t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7/B, B<sub>max</sub> = 0.7 ÷ 1.640 ns = 4.27 × 10⁸ bit/s = 427 Mbit/s.
Highest RZ rate: B<sub>max</sub> = 0.35 ÷ 1.640 ns = 213 Mbit/s, exactly half, because an RZ pulse occupies only half the slot.

Where the factors come from: a pulse whose edges take more than about 70 % of an NRZ slot no longer reaches its full level before the next bit begins, so the eye closes and inter-symbol interference rises. An RZ pulse lasts half a slot, so the same reasoning gives 35 %.

Each term in physical terms: the 0.6 ns source term is the laser or LED switching time; the 0.8 ns modal term is the spread of arrival times between modes in the multimode fiber; the 1.2 ns chromatic term is the spread between wavelengths of the source spectrum; the 0.5 ns receiver term corresponds to a bandwidth B<sub>rx</sub> = 350 ÷ 0.5 = 700 MHz.

Which term to attack: chromatic dispersion contributes 1.44 of the 2.69 ns², more than half. A narrower source (an LED of 40 nm replaced by a laser of a few nm) or operation near the zero-dispersion wavelength removes most of it.

If the chromatic term were removed completely, t<sub>sys</sub> = √(0.36 + 0.64 + 0.25) = √1.25 = 1.118 ns, and B<sub>max</sub> (NRZ) = 0.7 ÷ 1.118 ns = 626 Mbit/s, so 500 Mbit/s would pass with 1.40 − 1.12 = 0.28 ns to spare. Shortening the receiver rise time alone from 0.5 ns to 0.3 ns would give only √2.53 = 1.59 ns, still failing.

Note that adding the terms directly, 0.6 + 0.8 + 1.2 + 0.5 = 3.1 ns, would wrongly predict a limit of 226 Mbit/s; the quadrature sum is the correct combination for independent, near-Gaussian responses.
Closing check: at B = 427 Mbit/s, T<sub>b</sub> = 2.342 ns and 0.7 × 2.342 = 1.640 ns, equal to t<sub>sys</sub>, so 427 Mbit/s is the boundary.

bank.q: Design check for a 2.5 Gbit/s NRZ link over 80 km of standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm: DFB laser launching 0 dBm, spectral width 0.1 nm, rise time 40 ps; fiber 0.25 dB/km including splices, D = 17 ps/(nm·km); two connectors of 0.5 dB; APD receiver with sensitivity −32 dBm at 2.5 Gbit/s and rise time 100 ps; margin 6 dB. Check both budgets, find the attenuation-limited and dispersion-limited lengths, and name the binding limit.
outline: Power: available 32 dB, used 20 + 1 + 6 = 27 dB, spare 5 dB; received −21 dBm
Rise time: T<sub>b</sub> = 400 ps, allowance 280 ps; t<sub>chrom</sub> = 136 ps; t<sub>sys</sub> = 173.5 ps: passes
Loss binds; check rise time at 100 km (201 ps)
answer: The power budget closes with 5 dB spare. Received power = 0 − 21 = −21 dBm, 11 dB above the sensitivity.
Rise-time budget: T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ÷ (2.5 × 10⁹) = 400 ps; NRZ allowance 0.7 × 400 = 280 ps.
Fiber term: single-mode, so t<sub>mod</sub> = 0. t<sub>chrom</sub> = |D|Lσ<sub>λ</sub> = 17 × 80 × 0.1 = 136 ps.
173.5 ps ≤ 280 ps, so the rise-time budget passes with 106.5 ps to spare. At 80 km this link could even run at 0.7 ÷ 173.5 ps = 4.03 Gbit/s NRZ.
Attenuation-limited length: L<sub>att</sub> = (P<sub>T</sub> − P<sub>R</sub> − connectors − M) ÷ α = (32 − 1 − 6) ÷ 0.25 = 25 ÷ 0.25 = 100 km.
Dispersion-limited length: allowed fiber rise time = √(280² − 40² − 100²) = √(78 400 − 1600 − 10 000) = √66 800 = 258.5 ps; L<sub>disp</sub> = 258.5 ÷ (17 × 0.1) = 258.5 ÷ 1.7 = 152 km.
Binding limit: the reach is the smaller, L<sub>att</sub> = 100 km, so loss binds. The 80 km route is inside both limits.

The fiber-only estimate (165 km) is longer than the full-budget value (152 km), because the transmitter and receiver rise times use part of the 280 ps allowance. Always use the full budget for the final answer.

Remedies if the route grew past 100 km: an optical amplifier or a stronger laser lifts L<sub>att</sub>; dispersion would bind next at 152 km, after which a narrower source, dispersion-compensating fiber or a lower bit rate is needed.

Upgrade check: the same parts could not run at 10 Gbit/s, because the allowance would be 0.7 × 100 = 70 ps, already smaller than the receiver's own 100 ps rise time. At 80 km the parts top out at 0.7 ÷ 173.5 ps = 4.03 Gbit/s.

Closing check at 100 km: fiber loss 25 dB, received −26 dBm, exactly 6 dB above sensitivity (zero spare); t<sub>chrom</sub> = 170 ps and t<sub>sys</sub> = √(40² + 170² + 100²) = 201 ps, still under 280 ps, confirming that loss, not dispersion, sets the reach.

bank.q: In a far-field NA measurement on a step-index multimode fiber, the spot on a screen 10.0 cm from the fiber end is 4.25 cm across at the 5 % intensity edge. The core index is 1.48. Find the NA, the acceptance angle, the cladding index and Δ, and state the precautions that make the reading trustworthy.
outline: Set-up: fiber end, screen at D, spot diameter A at 5 % level
Precautions: overfilled steady launch, cladding-mode stripping, a few metres of fiber, 5 % not 50 %, screen square to the axis
answer: Set-up: light is launched into a few metres of fiber with an overfilled, steady launch; cladding modes are stripped; the output cone falls on a screen square to the fiber axis at distance D, and the spot diameter A is measured where the intensity is 5 % of the peak.
Geometry: the cone's half-angle θ<sub>a</sub> satisfies tan θ<sub>a</sub> = (A/2)/D, so sin θ<sub>a</sub> = (A/2)/√((A/2)² + D²) = A/√(A² + 4D²).
Acceptance angle: θ<sub>a</sub> = sin⁻¹ 0.208 = 12.0°. Check: tan θ<sub>a</sub> = 2.125 ÷ 10.0 = 0.2125 and tan⁻¹ 0.2125 = 12.0°. The full acceptance cone is 24.0°.

Relative index difference: Δ = (n<sub>1</sub> − n<sub>2</sub>) ÷ n<sub>1</sub> = (1.48 − 1.4653) ÷ 1.48 = 0.0099, about 1 %. Check with NA ≈ n<sub>1</sub>√(2Δ) = 1.48 × √0.0198 = 1.48 × 0.1407 = 0.208.

head: Precaution
Why
rows: An underfilled launch excites only low-order modes and gives too small an NA
Cladding light widens the spot and gives too large an NA
Use a few metres of fiber
Leaky modes die out, so the cone is set by the guided modes
The 50 % edge gives a smaller angle, not the NA
Screen square to the axis, D measured from the end face
A tilted screen or wrong D distorts A/D directly

answer: Alternative set-up: a detector on a rotating arm scans the far-field intensity against angle; θ<sub>a</sub> is read where the intensity has fallen to 5 % of the peak on each side, and the two half-angles are averaged to remove any tilt of the fiber end.

Use: NA sets how much light a source couples in and how sensitive the fiber is to bends. For a Lambertian LED butted to this step-index fiber the coupling efficiency is about NA² = 0.208² = 0.043, a loss of 10 log₁₀ 0.043 = −13.6 dB, which is why LEDs launch so little power.
Closing check: in water (n = 1.33) the same fiber accepts sin⁻¹(0.208/1.33) = 9.0°, smaller than in air, as expected since NA = n<sub>0</sub> sin θ.

bank.q: Describe the cut-back method with a neat set-up. A 5.0 km reel of single-mode fiber reads −21.85 dBm at 1310 nm; after cutting back to 2 m with the launch untouched it reads −20.10 dBm. Find α. The reel is then fitted with connectors and tested by insertion loss: the reference reading is −10.00 dBm and the reading through the reel is −12.95 dBm. Find the loss per connector. An OTDR shows the far-end reflection 49.0 µs after the pulse (n = 1.468); confirm the reel length.
outline: Set-up: source, mode scrambler, fiber, cladding-mode stripper, detector; cut without touching the launch
Insertion loss 2.95 dB = 1.75 fiber + 1.20 connectors: 0.60 dB each
OTDR z = ct/(2n) = 5.01 km
Precautions

answer.pre:
source → mode scrambler → long fiber L<sub>1</sub> → cladding-mode stripper → detector + power meter (P<sub>1</sub>)
(launch untouched) cut 2 m from the input → stripper → detector (P<sub>2</sub>)

answer: Procedure: read P<sub>1</sub> through the full length; cut the fiber about 2 m from the input without disturbing the launch; read P<sub>2</sub>. Launch and detector effects are identical in both readings and cancel.
Formula: α = 10 log₁₀(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>) ÷ (L<sub>1</sub> − L<sub>2</sub>). With readings in dBm, 10 log₁₀(P<sub>2</sub>/P<sub>1</sub>) is simply P<sub>2</sub>(dBm) − P<sub>1</sub>(dBm).
Loss of the removed length: −20.10 − (−21.85) = 1.75 dB. Removed length: 5.0 − 0.002 = 4.998 km.
α = 1.75 ÷ 4.998 = 0.350 dB/km, a normal value for single-mode fiber at 1310 nm.
0.60 dB per connector is inside the 0.3 to 1.0 dB planning range, so the connectors are acceptable but not premium.
OTDR length check: z = ct/(2n) = 3.0 × 10⁸ × 49.0 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ (2 × 1.468) = 14 700 ÷ 2.936 = 5007 m = 5.01 km, which agrees with the 5.0 km label to 0.1 %.

Why each part is there: the mode scrambler fills the modes the same way every time; the cladding-mode stripper removes light that would otherwise add to P<sub>2</sub> through the short length (it has not had distance to leak away); the large-area detector catches the whole output spot. With a lamp and monochromator in place of the source, α is found at many wavelengths and gives the loss spectrum of the fiber.

OTDR cross-check of α: on the raw (round-trip) backscatter, two points 5.0 km apart would differ by 2α × 5.0 = 2 × 0.350 × 5.0 = 3.50 dB; halving gives the one-way 1.75 dB and α = 0.350 dB/km, the same as the cut-back value.

Precautions: keep the launch untouched; use a mode scrambler and cladding-mode stripper; use a large-area detector so the spot is fully caught; cleave both ends square; keep the source power and temperature steady between the two readings.
Comparison: cut-back is destructive and suits the factory; insertion loss suits connectorised cable; the OTDR needs only one end and suits installed cable.
Closing check: the reel loss predicted from α and the connectors, 1.75 + 2 × 0.60 = 2.95 dB, equals the measured insertion loss.

bank.q: Compare the time-domain and frequency-domain methods of measuring fiber dispersion. A 0.4 ns pulse leaves 2.0 km of graded-index fiber 2.5 ns wide; find the fiber's bandwidth. A phase-shift set-up at 500 MHz reads a 122.4° change over 10 km when the wavelength steps from 1548 to 1552 nm; find D. Which method suits which fiber?
outline: Time domain: pulse broadening, τ = √(τ<sub>o</sub>² − τ<sub>i</sub>²), B<sub>opt</sub> ≈ 0.44/τ
Frequency domain: baseband response ratio, 3 dB point
Chromatic dispersion: pulse delay or phase shift against λ
Numbers: τ = 2.47 ns, B<sub>opt</sub> = 178 MHz, 357 MHz·km; Δτ = 680 ps, D = 17 ps/(nm·km)
Comparison table
answer: Time-domain (pulse-broadening) method: a narrow pulse from a laser is launched; a fast detector and sampling oscilloscope record its half-maximum width at the input (τ<sub>i</sub>, through a short reference length) and at the output (τ<sub>o</sub>). For near-Gaussian pulses the fiber's own broadening is τ = √(τ<sub>o</sub>² − τ<sub>i</sub>²) and its 3 dB optical bandwidth is B<sub>opt</sub> ≈ 0.44/τ.

answer.pre:
τ = √(2.5² − 0.4²) = √(6.25 − 0.16) = √6.09 = 2.47 ns
per km: 2.47 ÷ 2.0 = 1.23 ns/km
B<sub>opt</sub> = 0.44 ÷ 2.47 ns = 178 MHz
bandwidth-length product = 178 × 2.0 = 357 MHz·km

answer: Frequency-domain (baseband response) method: the source is modulated sinusoidally and the frequency is swept; the received power through the long fiber is divided by that through a short reference. The ratio H(f) is the fiber's frequency response, and the frequency where it falls by 3 dB (optical) is B<sub>opt</sub>, with no pulse-shape assumption.

Chromatic dispersion of single-mode fiber is too small to see as broadening of a short pulse, so the group delay is measured against wavelength: as arrival times (pulse-delay method) or as the phase of a modulated sine wave (phase-shift method), with Δφ = 360° × f<sub>m</sub> × Δτ.

17 ps/(nm·km) is the expected value for standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm. The phase change must stay below 360° over the step, or the phase wraps; 680 ps at 500 MHz is 0.34 of a period, so it is safe.

head: Point
Time domain
Frequency domain
rows: frequency response; 3 dB bandwidth directly; phase gives delay
picosecond pulses, fast detector, sampling scope
sine-modulated source, network or vector analyser
limited when τ<sub>o</sub> is close to τ<sub>i</sub>
multimode fiber with large modal spread

answer: Sources of error: in the time domain, a reference pulse width τ<sub>i</sub> close to τ<sub>o</sub> makes the subtraction inaccurate, and non-Gaussian shapes make 0.44/τ only approximate; in the phase-shift method, source wavelength error and phase wrap-round (Δφ beyond 360°) are the main risks, so the wavelength steps are kept small.

Judgement: for a graded-index multimode fiber the broadening (2.47 ns here) is large and the time-domain method is quick and direct. For a long single-mode link the spread per nanometre is only tens of picoseconds per kilometre, so the phase-shift method is preferred: it gives delay to a fraction of a picosecond without picosecond pulses.

Closing check: with the 357 MHz·km product, a 5 km run of this graded-index fiber would offer about 71 MHz (if bandwidth falls in proportion to length) of optical bandwidth, and the measured D predicts 17 × 10 × 4 = 680 ps over the step, matching the phase reading.

bank.q: Explain how an OTDR is used in the field for distance, attenuation, splice loss, fault location and reflectance. A splice reads 0.18 dB from end A and 0.02 dB from end B, and its echo returns 61.2 µs after the pulse (n = 1.468). A connector reflects 0.5 µW of 1 mW. Evaluate these readings.
outline: Principle: Rayleigh backscatter against time; z = ct/(2n)
Slope gives α (display is one-way)
Events: step for splice or bend, spike for connector or break; dead zone
Bidirectional averaging: 0.10 dB at 6.25 km
Reflectance −33 dB, ORL 33 dB: poor connector
Other field tools
answer: Principle: the OTDR launches short pulses and records the Rayleigh backscatter, plus reflections, against time. Light from distance z returns after t = 2nz/c, so the time axis becomes distance z = ct/(2n). The vertical axis is backscattered power in dB, displayed one-way (the raw round-trip slope 2α is halved).

head: Feature on the trace
Meaning
Read as
rows: step height = loss (averaged from both ends)
spike height gives reflectance, step gives loss
Flat blind stretch after a spike
events inside it cannot be read

answer: Splice loss: the two directions differ because the fibers on either side backscatter differently (different mode-field diameters). The error is equal and opposite from the two ends, so the true loss is the average: (0.18 + 0.02) ÷ 2 = 0.10 dB.

Evaluation: 0.10 dB equals the usual planning value for a fusion splice, so it is acceptable, but a reading of 0.18 dB from one end alone would have wrongly flagged it for re-splicing. A splice that reads as a gain from one end is not a fault; it is the same effect.
Reflectance of the connector: R = 10 log₁₀(0.5 × 10⁻⁶ ÷ 1 × 10⁻³) = 10 log₁₀(5 × 10⁻⁴) = −33.0 dB; its return loss is 33.0 dB.

Evaluation: a good polished connector reflects −50 dB or less, so −33 dB points to a dirty, damaged or air-gapped end face. Clean and inspect it; high reflections disturb lasers and add noise on high-speed and analog links.

Fault location: a break shows as a large spike (a clean cleave) or a sudden drop to noise; its distance comes from the same z = ct/(2n). Accuracy depends on the group index setting: a 1 % error in n gives a 1 % error in distance, 62 m at 6.25 km.

Why field readings differ from lab readings: the launch is not controlled, temperature and cable stress vary, bends in splice trays add loss, and one-direction readings are biased. Field crews therefore average both directions and confirm the total with a stable source and power meter, and use a visual fault locator for breaks near the ends.
Closing check: the average 0.10 dB lies between the two readings and the difference (0.18 − 0.02)/2 = 0.08 dB is the backscatter bias, the same magnitude in both directions.

bank.q: Why do cutoff wavelength and fiber diameter matter in single-mode link design? Describe how each is measured, and analyze a bend-reference result whose ratio is 0.25 dB at 1240 nm, 0.10 dB at 1270 nm and 0.02 dB at 1300 nm.
outline: Below cutoff LP<sub>11</sub> also travels: modal noise and dispersion
Bend-reference method: 2 m loose loop vs small stripping loop; 0.1 dB criterion
Fiber cutoff vs cable cutoff (≤ 1260 nm)
Reading: λ<sub>c</sub> = 1270 nm (2 m); single-mode at 1310 nm; cable cutoff lower
Diameter: microscope, shadow scan, near field; offsets cause joint loss
answer: Why cutoff matters: the fiber must carry only LP<sub>01</sub> at the working wavelength. If a second mode (LP<sub>11</sub>) also travels, the two arrive at different times (modal dispersion) and interfere at joints (modal noise), so the loss and the BER become unstable. The operating wavelength must lie above the cutoff wavelength.

Bend-reference method: a 2 m sample is laid in one loose loop and its transmitted power is recorded against wavelength from a lamp and monochromator. The scan is repeated with a small extra loop that strips LP<sub>11</sub> at all wavelengths. The ratio of the two (in dB) is flat at long wavelengths and rises below cutoff, where the loose fiber still delivers LP<sub>11</sub> power.
Criterion: λ<sub>c</sub> is the wavelength where the ratio is 0.1 dB above its flat long-wavelength level.

answer.text: Reading the given result (flat level taken as about 0 dB):

head: Wavelength (nm)
Ratio (dB)
Meaning
rows: LP<sub>11</sub> still carries power: below cutoff

answer: Analysis: the 2 m fiber cutoff is 1270 nm. That is above the 1260 nm cable limit of standard fiber, but cable cutoff is measured on longer, bent lengths and is always shorter than the 2 m value, so the cabled fiber may still meet ≤ 1260 nm; the cable cutoff test must decide. Either way the fiber is single-mode at 1310 nm and 1550 nm.

Why diameter matters: a joint aligns two fibers by their claddings. If the cladding diameter or the core concentricity is off, the cores are offset and every splice and connector loses more. A 125 µm cladding held to about ±1 µm keeps connector loss within the budget's planning values.

How diameter is measured: the cladding diameter and concentricity from a calibrated video-microscope image of the cleaved end face; during drawing, by scanning a laser beam across the fiber and timing its shadow; the core diameter from the near-field intensity across the end face or from a refracted near-field index profile.
Effect on design: cutoff decides which windows are single-mode; diameter and concentricity decide joint loss in the power budget.
Closing check: the ratio falls 0.15 dB from 1240 to 1270 nm and 0.08 dB from 1270 to 1300 nm, flattening as expected above cutoff, so the 1270 nm reading sits on the knee of the curve.

bank.q: Case study: a 100 Mbit/s NRZ link must cover 8 km. Design A uses an 850 nm LED (−16 dBm launched, 40 nm wide, rise time 6 ns) on graded-index multimode fiber (3.0 dB/km, |D| = 90 ps/(nm·km), B<sub>0</sub> = 500 MHz·km, q = 0.7). Design B uses a 1310 nm Fabry–Perot laser (−3 dBm, 2 nm wide, rise time 0.5 ns) on single-mode fiber (0.4 dB/km, |D| = 2 ps/(nm·km)). Both use a pin receiver (sensitivity −35 dBm, overload −8 dBm, bandwidth 100 MHz), two connectors (1.0 dB each for A, 0.5 dB each for B) and a 6 dB margin. Evaluate both designs with the power and rise-time budgets and recommend one.
outline: Allowance: T<sub>b</sub> = 10 ns, t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 7 ns; t<sub>rx</sub> = 3.5 ns
A power: available 19 dB, used 32 dB, spare −13 dB
A rise: t<sub>chrom</sub> 28.8 ns, t<sub>mod</sub> 3.77 ns, t<sub>sys</sub> 29.9 ns: fails
B power: available 32 dB, used 10.2 dB, spare 21.8 dB; received −7.2 dBm above overload: add attenuator
B rise: t<sub>sys</sub> 3.54 ns: passes; B<sub>max</sub> 198 Mbit/s
Recommend B with a fixed attenuator
answer: Common numbers: T<sub>b</sub> = 1 ÷ (100 × 10⁶) = 10 ns, so t<sub>sys</sub> ≤ 0.7 × 10 = 7.0 ns. Receiver rise time t<sub>rx</sub> = 350 ÷ 100 = 3.5 ns for both designs.
Design A fails the power budget by 13 dB: even with no margin the received −42 dBm is 7 dB below the −35 dBm sensitivity. Its longest span would be (19 − 2 − 6) ÷ 3.0 = 3.7 km.

Design B closes with 21.8 dB spare, but −7.2 dBm is above the −8 dBm overload level, so the receiver would saturate. A fixed 3 dB attenuator brings it to −10.2 dBm, inside the window, and leaves 18.8 dB spare.

Design A also fails the rise-time budget by a factor of four: the LED's 40 nm spectrum on 850 nm fiber gives 28.8 ns of chromatic spreading, far more than the modal term. A faster receiver cannot cure it.

Design B passes with 3.46 ns to spare. Its system rise time is almost entirely the receiver (3.5 ns); at 1310 nm the fiber is near zero dispersion, so the laser's 2 nm width costs only 32 ps over 8 km.

Recommendation: Design B with a 3 dB attenuator. It meets both budgets with large reserves, and the same fiber could later carry about 198 Mbit/s with this receiver, or more with a faster one. Design A would need repeaters every 3.7 km and still could not reach 100 Mbit/s.

What would rescue Design A: shortening the span is not enough on its own, because the chromatic term alone at 3.7 km is 0.090 × 3.7 × 40 = 13.3 ns, still above 7 ns. It needs a narrow source (a laser) as well as a lower-loss window, which is Design B.
Cost note: Design A's parts are cheaper per end, but it fails both budgets; the extra cost of a 1310 nm laser and single-mode connectors is the price of meeting the specification.
Closing check for B after the attenuator: losses 3.2 + 1.0 + 3.0 = 7.2 dB, received −10.2 dBm, which is 24.8 dB above sensitivity and 2.2 dB below overload; t<sub>sys</sub> = 3.54 ns ≤ 7.0 ns.

A photodiode with internal gain; about 5 to 10 dB more sensitive than a pin photodiode, at the cost of a high bias voltage.
Time taken by one bit, T<sub>b</sub> = 1/B.
Cutoff of the fiber in its cable; shorter than the 2 m fiber cutoff, at most 1260 nm for standard single-mode fiber.
A short section that removes light travelling in the cladding before a measurement.

glossary.term: Composite second order (CSO) and composite triple beat (CTB)
glossary.def: Distortion products from two and three subcarriers mixing in a multichannel analog link.
Attenuation measurement that reads the power through a long fiber and then through a short piece of it, with the launch untouched.
Length after a strong reflection on an OTDR trace in which no other event can be read.
Change of group delay with wavelength per unit length, in ps/(nm·km).
Extra received power needed to hold the BER when dispersion closes the eye.
Intensity of the light leaving the fiber, measured far from the end face against angle.
Loss test that compares a reference reading through a short cord with a reading through the cable under test.
A device that fills the fiber's modes in a fixed, repeatable way at the launch.
Sine of the acceptance half-angle; NA = √(n<sub>1</sub>² − n<sub>2</sub>²).
Incident over reflected power in dB, a positive number; higher is better.
Optical time-domain reflectometer: sends pulses and plots backscatter against distance to show loss and events.
Largest received power a receiver accepts before saturating.
Chromatic dispersion measurement that reads the phase of a modulated signal as the wavelength is stepped.
Smallest mean received power that gives the required BER at the bit rate.
Reflected over incident power at one joint, in dB; a negative number.
Laser power fluctuation relative to the mean power, in dB/Hz.
Time a response takes to go from 10 % to 90 % of its final value.
Range of wavelengths a source emits; it multiplies with D and L to spread a pulse.
Decibels held back in the power budget for ageing, temperature and repairs.
A red laser source whose light leaks out at a break or tight bend, showing where it is.
